job.style: a comparison of two related ideas

passage: In India, secularism is defined by the principle of 'principled distance,' which allows the state to maintain a neutral stance while still engaging with religious communities. Unlike some Western models that demand a complete wall of separation, the Indian state can intervene to ensure equality and protect individual rights. For instance, the government may provide financial aid to religious schools to promote education, provided this support is offered without discrimination. Furthermore, the state can step in to stop harmful practices, such as untouchability or child marriage, even if they are rooted in religious traditions. This does not mean the state is anti-religious or trying to abolish faith. Instead, it means the government respects the freedom of all citizens to practice their beliefs while ensuring that no single religion dominates or violates the fundamental rights of others. By allowing religious symbols and festivals in public life, India demonstrates that secularism is about fostering harmony rather than erasing religion from the public sphere. The state acts as a referee, ensuring that religious freedom is balanced with the values of justice and equality for every citizen.

items.evidence: Furthermore, the state can step in to stop harmful practices, such as untouchability or child marriage, even if they are rooted in religious traditions.
items.q: Why can the Indian state act against child marriage even when a religion's tradition supports it?
options: Protecting people's rights matters more than tradition
Every religion's customs must be approved by the state
Religious matters are never the state's concern
The state wants to reduce the role of faith
items.explain: The state may step in to stop harmful practices, even religious ones, to protect individual rights and equality.

wrong.why: thinks the state must approve all customs
thinks the state must never interfere in religion
thinks the state is against religion

items.evidence: For instance, the government may provide financial aid to religious schools to promote education, provided this support is offered without discrimination.
items.q: A state gives grants to schools run by different faiths, on equal terms. Is this secular?
options: Yes, because the aid is fair to every faith
Yes, because the state backs the largest faith
No, because the state is funding religious groups
No, because only government schools may get aid
items.explain: Aid to religious schools is acceptable when given without discrimination, because it promotes education fairly.

wrong.why: thinks the state helps its favourite religion
thinks funding a religious school is not secular
thinks the state must avoid all religious involvement

items.evidence: By allowing religious symbols and festivals in public life, India demonstrates that secularism is about fostering harmony rather than erasing religion from the public sphere.
items.q: Students celebrate several festivals openly at a government school. What does this show about Indian secularism?
options: It aims to build harmony, not remove faith
It requires every student to join each festival
It bans symbols belonging to the majority group
It treats the majority's festivals as most important
items.explain: Allowing festivals in public life shows secularism fosters harmony instead of erasing religion from public spaces.

wrong.why: confuses freedom to celebrate with a duty to join
thinks secularism bans religious symbols in public
thinks majority festivals can take priority and stay secular

items.evidence: The state acts as a referee, ensuring that religious freedom is balanced with the values of justice and equality for every citizen.
items.q: How is the state's role as a 'referee' different from staying away from religion completely?
options: It steps in to keep freedom and fairness balanced
It picks the religion it finds most useful
It stays out of religion in every situation
It makes sure all citizens follow one faith
items.explain: A referee does not stay away; it keeps religious freedom balanced with justice and equality for everyone.

wrong.why: thinks the state helps the religion it likes
thinks the state never gets involved with any religion
thinks a secular country has one shared religion
